items.title: Lip–voice phase consistency for audio-visual deepfakes
items.authors: Seed idea — validate novelty before use
items.inshort: Most AV deepfake detectors compare lips and audio at the content level. Check whether the timing (phase) of mouth openings and speech energy stay locked; many lip-sync generators drift by a few frames.

slides.title: The gap
slides.text: Detectors often learn generator artifacts, not physical constraints that any fake must satisfy.

slides.title: Method sketch
flow: Estimate cross-correlation and phase drift per window
Small temporal transformer on drift features

slides.title: Experiments
points: FakeAVCeleb, AV-Deepfake1M
Cross-generator test
AUC + localization of fake segments

slides.title: Risks
slides.text: Good lip-sync generators may already align phase; dubbed real videos could be false positives.

items.title: Diffusion-forged signatures: a new threat to offline verification
items.authors: Seed idea — validate novelty before use
items.inshort: Writer-conditioned diffusion models can produce skilled-looking signatures from a few samples. Build a benchmark of such forgeries and test whether current offline verifiers are fooled.

slides.title: The gap
slides.text: Signature verification benchmarks mostly contain human skilled forgeries, not generative ones.

slides.title: Experiments
points: CEDAR, GPDS-style datasets
EER under human vs. generated forgeries
Ablation: shots per writer

items.title: Watermarks that survive regeneration attacks via semantic anchoring
items.authors: Seed idea — validate novelty before use
items.inshort: Diffusion regeneration wipes pixel-level watermarks. Tie part of the message to semantic layout (object positions, coarse structure) that regeneration preserves, and decode it jointly with the pixel mark.

slides.title: The gap
slides.text: Pixel watermarks are robust to classic edits but not to 'redraw the image' attacks.

slides.title: Method sketch
flow: Semantic channel: tiny structured perturbation of layout features
Train against regeneration in the loop

slides.title: Experiments
points: Regeneration with SD/VAE attacks
Bit accuracy & TPR@1%FPR
Image quality: PSNR/LPIPS

items.title: Watermark Anything with Localized Messages
items.authors: T. Sander, P. Fernandez, A. Durmus, T. Furon, M. Douze
items.inshort: WAM treats watermarking as a segmentation problem: every pixel tells you whether it is watermarked and which message it carries. So it can find small watermarked regions inside an edited or spliced image and even read several different messages from one picture.

slides.title: Why do we need this?
slides.text: Classic watermarking hides one message in the whole image. Real images get cropped, spliced and inpainted, so a global decoder fails when only part of the image keeps the mark.

slides.title: Key points
points: Embedder hides a message imperceptibly; extractor predicts a per-pixel mask and per-pixel bits
Two-stage training: robustness first, then imperceptibility and multiple watermarks
Can localise watermarked areas and decode several distinct messages in one image

slides.title: What's new
slides.text: Re-framing watermark extraction as dense (pixel-level) prediction instead of a single global decode.

slides.title: Main results
points: Competitive robustness with prior methods on standard image edits
Locates watermarked regions even when they cover a small part of the image
Recovers multiple separate messages from one image

slides.title: Limitations
slides.text: Very aggressive generative edits that redraw the region can still remove the mark; payload per region is small.

slides.title: Explain like I'm new
slides.text: Imagine stamping tiny invisible ink dots everywhere on a photo. If someone cuts out a piece, you can still scan each piece and say 'this bit is mine, and it says hello'.

items.title: Proactive Detection of Voice Cloning with Localized Watermarking (AudioSeal)
items.authors: R. San Roman, P. Fernandez, A. Défossez, T. Furon, T. Tran, H. Elsahar
items.inshort: AudioSeal marks AI-generated speech at the moment it is created, then a detector finds that mark sample-by-sample. This turns voice-clone detection from guessing artifacts into checking a hidden signature, and it is fast enough for large-scale use.

slides.title: Why do we need this?
slides.text: Passive audio-deepfake detectors chase artifacts that vanish as generators improve. A proactive mark added at generation time gives a reliable signal.

slides.title: Key points
points: Generator adds an imperceptible watermark to speech
Detector outputs a per-sample probability of being watermarked
Localized: finds watermarked segments in longer audio
Optional multi-bit message to identify the model version

slides.title: What's new
slides.text: Sample-level localized detection with a perceptual loudness loss, trained jointly with a detector, designed for speed.

slides.title: Main results
points: Robust to many common audio edits
Detection is much faster than earlier audio watermark decoders
Localization works on short marked segments

slides.title: Limitations
slides.text: Only protects audio from generators that choose to embed the mark; adaptive removal attacks remain an open risk.

slides.title: Explain like I'm new
slides.text: It's like a radio station adding an ultrasonic 'beep' only machines can hear — later, any clip can be checked for the beep, second by second.

items.title: The Stable Signature: Rooting Watermarks in Latent Diffusion Models
items.authors: P. Fernandez, G. Couairon, H. Jégou, M. Douze, T. Furon
items.inshort: Instead of watermarking images after generation, Stable Signature fine-tunes the diffusion model's latent decoder so every image it produces already carries a hidden signature. Each user can get a differently fine-tuned decoder, enabling attribution.

slides.title: Why do we need this?
slides.text: Post-hoc watermarks on open-source generators are easy to skip — just delete the watermark line of code. The mark needs to live inside the model weights.

slides.title: Key points
points: Pre-train a watermark extractor (HiDDeN-style)
Fine-tune only the VAE decoder so outputs decode to a fixed message
Different users can get different decoders
Detection by statistical test on extracted bits

slides.title: What's new
slides.text: Merging the watermark into the generator's decoder weights, making generation and marking inseparable.

slides.title: Architecture
flow: Text prompt → diffusion in latent space

slides.title: Main results
points: Mark survives common edits such as crops and compression
Image quality stays close to the original model
Supports detection and user identification

slides.title: Limitations
slides.text: Strong regeneration/purification attacks and model fine-tuning can weaken the mark.

slides.title: Explain like I'm new
slides.text: Rather than signing each painting after it's done, you change the painter's brush so every stroke secretly contains the signature.

items.title: TruFor: Leveraging All-Round Clues for Trustworthy Image Forgery Detection and Localization
items.authors: F. Guillaro, D. Cozzolino, A. Sud, N. Dufour, L. Verdoliva
items.inshort: TruFor combines the RGB image with a learned camera-noise fingerprint (Noiseprint++) to detect and localize forgeries, and it also outputs a confidence map so you know where its decision can be trusted, reducing false alarms.

slides.title: Why do we need this?
slides.text: Forgery detectors often fire on harmless regions and give no sense of how reliable their localization is.

slides.title: Key points
points: Noiseprint++: self-supervised noise fingerprint robust to compression
Transformer-based fusion of RGB + noise features
Outputs anomaly map, confidence map and global integrity score

slides.title: What's new
slides.text: A reliability (confidence) map learned jointly with localization, plus an improved Noiseprint++ extractor.

slides.title: Main results
points: Strong localization and detection across many forgery benchmarks
Handles cheap-fakes and AI-based manipulations
Confidence map lowers false positives

slides.title: Limitations
slides.text: Heavy post-processing and fully generated images remain harder; noise cues weaken after strong recompression.

slides.title: Explain like I'm new
slides.text: It looks at both the picture and the camera's invisible 'fingerprint grain'. Where the grain pattern breaks, something was pasted — and it tells you how sure it is.

items.title: Towards Universal Fake Image Detectors that Generalize Across Generative Models
items.authors: U. Ojha, Y. Li, Y. J. Lee
items.inshort: Detectors trained on GAN fakes fail on diffusion fakes. This paper skips learning a fake-detector from scratch and uses frozen CLIP features with a tiny classifier (nearest neighbour or linear probe), which generalizes far better to unseen generators.

slides.title: Why do we need this?
slides.text: A real-vs-fake classifier trained end-to-end learns artifacts of its training generator and treats everything else as 'real'.

slides.title: Key points
points: Use a frozen large pretrained feature space (CLIP ViT)
Train only a linear probe or use nearest neighbour
Test on many unseen generator families

slides.title: What's new
slides.text: Showing that a feature space not trained for fake detection generalizes better than one that is.

slides.title: Main results
points: Large gains on unseen generators vs. trained-from-scratch detectors
Works with very simple classifiers
Became a standard baseline (UnivFD)

slides.title: Limitations
slides.text: Can be sensitive to post-processing; newer generators keep testing its limits.

slides.title: Explain like I'm new
slides.text: Instead of memorising one forger's mistakes, ask a well-travelled expert (CLIP) who has seen millions of real photos to tell you what looks 'off'.

items.title: FaceForensics++: Learning to Detect Manipulated Facial Images
items.authors: A. Rössler, D. Cozzolino, L. Verdoliva, C. Riess, J. Thies, M. Nießner
items.inshort: FaceForensics++ is the benchmark that kick-started deepfake detection: videos manipulated with four methods at several compression levels, plus a hidden test benchmark. It showed that learned detectors beat humans, especially on compressed video.

slides.title: Why do we need this?
slides.text: Without a large shared dataset, detection results were not comparable and could not train deep models.

slides.title: Key points
points: Four manipulations: Deepfakes, Face2Face, FaceSwap, NeuralTextures
Raw, high-quality and low-quality compression levels
Human study vs. learned detectors
Hidden-label benchmark for fair comparison

slides.title: What's new
slides.text: A large-scale, multi-method, multi-compression benchmark with standardized evaluation.

slides.title: Main results
points: Learned detectors clearly outperform human observers
Accuracy drops a lot under heavy compression
Domain-specific face crops help

slides.title: Limitations
slides.text: Older manipulation methods; models trained only on FF++ generalize poorly to new deepfakes.

slides.title: Explain like I'm new
slides.text: Like building a big exam with answer keys so every lie-detector can be tested on the same questions.

items.title: ArcFace: Additive Angular Margin Loss for Deep Face Recognition
items.authors: J. Deng, J. Guo, N. Xue, S. Zafeiriou
items.inshort: ArcFace adds a fixed angular margin to the softmax loss so face embeddings of the same person cluster tightly on a hypersphere while different people are pushed apart. Simple to implement, it became the default loss for face recognition.

slides.title: Why do we need this?
slides.text: Plain softmax separates classes but doesn't make embeddings compact enough for open-set face verification.

slides.title: Key points
points: Normalize features and class weights → cosine similarity
Add margin m to the angle of the true class
Scale by s before softmax
Clear geometric meaning on the hypersphere

slides.title: What's new
slides.text: An additive angular margin, cos(θ + m), which has a constant geodesic-distance interpretation.

slides.title: Main results
points: Strong results across major face verification benchmarks
Stable training, little overhead
Widely adopted via InsightFace

slides.title: Limitations
slides.text: Sensitive to label noise; margin and scale need tuning.

slides.title: Explain like I'm new
slides.text: Faces are points on a ball. ArcFace insists each person's points stay in their own slice of the ball with an extra 'buffer zone' between neighbours.

items.title: AASIST: Audio Anti-Spoofing using Integrated Spectro-Temporal Graph Attention Networks
items.authors: J.-w. Jung, H.-S. Heo, H. Tak, H.-j. Shim, J. S. Chung, B.-J. Lee, H.-J. Yu, N. Evans
items.inshort: AASIST detects spoofed (synthetic or converted) speech from the raw waveform by modelling spectral and temporal artifacts as two graphs and fusing them with a heterogeneous graph attention layer. It is compact and became a go-to baseline for audio deepfake detection.

slides.title: Why do we need this?
slides.text: Spoofing artifacts can hide in specific frequency bands or time segments; separate models for each are clumsy.

slides.title: Key points
points: Raw-waveform front-end (RawNet2-style sinc filters)
Spectral graph + temporal graph
Heterogeneous stacking graph attention
Max graph operation for competing branches

slides.title: What's new
slides.text: A single model that integrates spectral and temporal graphs through heterogeneous graph attention.

slides.title: Main results
points: Strong results on ASVspoof 2019 LA
Lightweight variant (AASIST-L) stays competitive
Common baseline in later challenges

slides.title: Limitations
slides.text: Trained on ASVspoof-style attacks; generalization to new TTS/VC systems and codecs needs extra data.

slides.title: Explain like I'm new
slides.text: It listens to the voice twice — once as 'which pitches look weird' and once as 'which moments sound weird' — then lets the two notes talk to each other.
